title: Dry ice never melts: it skips straight from solid to gas
body: Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide, and at ordinary air pressure CO₂ has no liquid form at all. Warm a block and it **sublimes**, turning directly into gas at −78.5 °C and leaving no puddle, which is where the name comes from. Liquid CO₂ exists only above about 5.1 atmospheres of pressure. The spooky fog it makes in a bowl of water isn’t the CO₂ itself, which is invisible: the escaping gas chills the water and drags tiny droplets of it into the air.

slides.alt: A phase diagram of carbon dioxide with temperature across and pressure up. The solid, liquid and gas regions meet at the triple point at 5.1 atmospheres and minus 56.4 degrees Celsius. A dashed line at 1 atmosphere crosses straight from solid to gas at minus 78.5 degrees.
slides.caption: At 1 atm the line from solid runs straight into gas; liquid only appears above 5.1 atm.

slides.question: At normal air pressure, at what temperature does dry ice turn to gas?
slides.explanation: −78.5 °C. Below about 5.1 atmospheres carbon dioxide has no liquid state, so the solid goes straight to gas.

slides.label: where dry ice turns straight into gas at normal pressure
slides.text: That is why it keeps things cold without any meltwater.

slides.question: How cold was the coldest air ever recorded on Earth, at Vostok Station in Antarctica in 1983?
slides.explanation: −89.2 °C, on 21 July 1983: colder than dry ice at −78.5 °C, though nowhere near the −183 °C and −195.8 °C at which liquid oxygen and liquid nitrogen boil.

slides.heading: Where does the fog come from?

left.label: Common guess
left.text: It’s the carbon dioxide gas you can see.

right.label: Actually
right.text: CO₂ gas is invisible. The fog is tiny droplets of water from the bowl, chilled by the escaping gas.

slides.heading: A 19th-century surprise
slides.text: Solid carbon dioxide was first observed in 1835 by the French inventor Adrien-Jean-Pierre Thilorier. The name ‘Dry ice’ began as a trademark of the DryIce Corporation of America, and like many trademarks it became the everyday word.
